“Tell me what is on your mind.”

“I have a cousin, my sole relative and an orphan like myself, whom I love dearly. She is five years younger than I, living in a farmer’s house in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has become of me—for I cannot write—and if I could, how should I explain it? It is better left so.”

“Yes, yes: better as it stands.”

“What I was thinking as we came along, and still think now as I look into your kind, strong face that gives me so much courage, is this:—If the Republic truly benefits the poor, if they grow less hungry and suffer less in every way, she might live many years; she might even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you suppose”—the patient eyes, so full of endurance, brim with tears, the lips part more and tremble—“that it will feel long to me, waiting for her in that better land where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot, my child; there is no Time there, no hardship there.”

“You comfort me so deeply! I am so ignorant. Should I kiss you now? Has the moment arrived?”

“Yes.”

She touches his lips; he touches hers; they bless each other solemnly. The slender hand is steady as he lets it go; nothing but a sweet, bright constancy shows in the patient face. She steps forward ahead of him—then she is gone; the knitting women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.”

The murmur of countless voices, countless faces turning upward, the surge of many footsteps along the crowd’s edge, until it swells forward in one mass, like a single great heave of water, all vanish in a flash. Twenty-Three.

{"request_id":"c0e898d2e5ed8106031263bd","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse, attractive, quick-witted, and wealthy, settled in a comfortable home and blessed with cheerful spirits, appeared to combine several of existence’s best favors; and she had spent nearly twenty-one years in the world with scarcely anything to grieve or annoy her.

She was the younger of two daughters belonging to a truly affectionate, indulgent father; and, due to her sister’s marriage, had presided over his household from a very early age. Her mother had been gone too long for her to recollect more than a vague impression of those tender embraces; and her place had been filled by an excellent woman as governess, who had fallen little short of a mother in her affection.

For sixteen years Miss Taylor had been a member of Mr. Woodhouse’s family, acting less as a governess than as a companion, warmly attached to both daughters, though especially to Emma. Between the two it was a relationship more like that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had relinquished the nominal post of governess, her gentle temper had scarcely permitted her to enforce restraint; and, the slightest remnant of authority having long since vanished, they had gone on living together as friend with friend, deeply attached, with Emma doing precisely what she pleased; valuing Miss Taylor’s judgment highly, yet principally guided by her own.

The genuine drawbacks, indeed, in Emma’s circumstances were the ease of obtaining rather too completely her own will and an inclination to think just a trifle too favorably of herself; these were the imperfections that threatened to tarnish her many delights. Nevertheless, the hazard was at present so little recognized that she did not consider them in the least as misfortunes.

Sorrow arrived—a gentle sorrow—but not at all in the form of any unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor’s departure that first brought Emma grief. On the wedding-day of this treasured friend, Emma first sat absorbed in mournful reflection of more than a moment. Once the ceremony ended and the bridal party departed, her father and she were left to dine alone, with no expectation of a third to enliven the long evening. Her father composed himself to sleep after dinner as usual, and she had then only to sit and dwell on what she had lost.
